To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

oxytocin and arginine vasopressin control the firing pattern in their respective magnocellular hypothalamo-hypophysial neurones in a way that favours the patterns of activity best suited for efficient systemic hormone release.
oxytocin enhances the amplitude and frequency of bursts in oxytocin neurones, whereas vasopressin decreases the amplitude and duration of bursts in vasopressin neurons.
oxytocin and arginine vasopressin control their respective neurone firing patterns by acting on soma and dendrites in the hypothalamic magnocellular nuclei.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the control of firing pattern in oxytocin (OXT) and vasopression (AVP) neurons.
the study of the mechanisms involved in the regulation of hormone secretion.
the study of the control of the firing pattern of hypothalamic magnocellular neurones.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the firing pattern autocontrol of OT and AVP neurones is a complex process, which involves several mechanisms, and which is finely tuned to the physiological needs of the animal, and to the specificities of the hormones involved.
OT and AVP are not only the hormones of lactation and water homeostasis, but also the autocontrol factors of their respective neurones.

the firing pattern of oxytocin (OXT) neurons is controlled by the OXT released from soma and/or dendrites within the supraoptic nucleus (SON) and the paraventricular nucleus (PVN), while the firing pattern of vasopressin neurons is controlled by vasopressin itself released from dendrites.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hypothalamic magnocellular system is a model for the study of neuronal self-regulation.
OT and AVP are involved in the control of their own secretion by acting on the firing patterns of their respective neurones.
OT and AVP act in a complementary manner, each hormone controlling the firing pattern of its own neurones in a way which optimises systemic hormone release.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the activity of OT and AVP neurones is not only controlled by their respective releasing hormones but also by each other.
the firing pattern is not a simple reflection of the hormone concentration but is actively controlled by the hormones.
OT and AVP act as autocontrollers of phasic activity in their respective neurones.
